modules.cost: 4 + 3 + 6 + 6 + 10 = 29 predicate calls per input, each constant time, and at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes read.
modules.does: [`decode`] turns a fuzzer's bytes into grid points with `geom-test`'s [`GridSampler`] (four 2D points, then five 3D points). [`harness`] calls every exact predicate on them: `orient2d`, `incircle`, `orient3d` and `insphere`. For each, it checks that the predicate answers, then swaps every pair of points and checks that the sign flips, `Zero` staying `Zero`.
guarantees: **Any bytes are a case.** Every byte string, the empty one included, decodes to valid grid points (magnitude at most 2^40 − 1), aimed at the hard cases: extremes of the frame, repeated and one-step-apart points, collinear points and coarse sub-grids (see `geom_test::grid`).
**A bounded input.** [`decode`] reads at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes; longer inputs only add bytes nobody reads. The bound is derived below and a unit test builds the input that reaches it.
**A panic is a failure.** The harness does not catch panics: a predicate that panics fails the run, and bolero reports the input and its seed.

**An error is a failure.** Each predicate returns `Result<Sign, NumError>`, and `geom-num` proves that for grid points it is always `Ok`: its bit budgets are derived for every grid input and checked when it compiles, so `NumError::BudgetExceeded` can only be a defect in `geom-num` (`geom_num::predicate`'s module documentation). Every point the harness decodes is a grid point, so an error, on the first call or after any swap, is a [`Finding`] naming the predicate, the error and the points. It is never read as a sign, so a defect can never pass for an exact degeneracy or for a sign that flipped.
**A broken law is a [`Finding`]** naming the predicate, the swap and the points.

method.text: the algebraic laws of section 28.6 of the kernel architecture (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`, "Swapping two points flips the sign"). Each predicate is the sign of a determinant with one row per point (the points lifted onto the paraboloid z = |p|² for in-circle and in-sphere), as in Shewchuk, "Adaptive Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic and Fast Robust Geometric Predicates", Discrete & Computational Geometry 18, 1997 (<https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009321>), which `geom_num::predicate` follows. Exchanging two points exchanges two rows, and by the Leibniz formula an exchange of two rows negates a determinant, so every transposition must flip the sign. The board names orient2d's swap; the same law is checked on the other three predicates, whose points the harness decodes anyway.

method.text: Euclid's algorithm for the greatest common divisor (Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, volume 2, section 4.5.2, Algorithm A; <https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html>), with cross-cancellation before multiplying (Knuth 4.5.1), so intermediate products stay as small as the result allows. A fraction in lowest terms has a finite decimal expansion exactly when its denominator is 2^a × 5^b, and then it has max(a, b) digits after the point (Hardy and Wright, *An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers*, section 9.2); the unit tests check both facts on every denominator that divides 6,400.

modules.cost: every generator once, plus reading or writing each output and listing each generated folder (at most [`MAX_FOLDER_DEPTH`] folders deep, without recursion). Validation compares every pair of outputs and of folders: O(n²) in their number, times their length.
modules.does: [`validate`] checks a registry's rules. [`write()`] produces every output and writes each one whose bytes changed. [`check`] produces every output in memory and compares it with the file, byte for byte, reporting each as current, different (with the first line that differs) or missing. Both also report every orphan: a file in a generated folder that no generator owns. Both work on a workspace root given by the caller, so tests can use a scratch copy.
guarantees: **Byte for byte.** `check` compares bytes, not text: a changed line end, a trailing space or a missing final newline is a difference.

**Validated and generated before anything is written.** `write` validates the registry and runs every generator before it writes any file, so a broken registry or a failing generator leaves every file as it was. An I/O error part-way (a full disk, a folder where a file should be) can leave the outputs before it written; `write` returns the error, and running it again once the cause is fixed finishes the job, because it rewrites only what differs.
**Every file is reported.** `check` does not stop at the first difference: the report names every output that differs or is missing, and every orphan.

**No orphans.** Every output lies inside one of the registry's generated folders ([`Folder`]), and every file in such a folder must be the output of a registered generator or on the folder's keep list. So the old output of a renamed or removed generator is reported as [`Status::Orphan`] until someone deletes it. Neither `write` nor `check` deletes anything.

**One file per output, on every system CI runs.** An output path is relative, uses `/`, and has only plain components of the portable filename character set (`A`–`Z`, `a`–`z`, `0`–`9`, `.`, `_`, `-`), none longer than 255 bytes, none starting with `-` or ending with `.`, and none a Windows device name (`CON`, `PRN`, `AUX`, `NUL`, `COM0`–`COM9`, `LPT0`–`LPT9`, in any case, with or without an extension); the whole path is at most [`MAX_OUTPUT_LEN`] bytes. No two outputs are equal when letter case is ignored (Windows and macOS file systems ignore it), and no output lies inside another. So two generators can never write one file on any runner, and every output can be a file.

errors.name: NumError

invariants: Every grid coordinate is a whole number of grid steps with magnitude at most [`grid::COORD_MAX`] (2^40 − 1). Every exact predicate's bit budget assumes this, and each predicate's doc comment carries its derivation, whose arithmetic is asserted when the crate compiles.

Every predicate returns a [`sign::Sign`], never a number, and is exact: no rounding decides a sign. A computation that cannot complete is reported as [`NumError::BudgetExceeded`], never answered; no input can cause one, only a defect in this crate.
A [`plane::Plane`] and a [`plane::Tpi`] check their bit budgets when they are made, so every computation on them fits its type.

Committing a three-plane point to the grid ([`plane::Tpi::to_grid`]) rounds each coordinate to the nearest step, ties to even, moving it by at most half a step ([`ladder::COMMIT_PER_AXIS`]), and says whether it moved.

Integer arithmetic on fixed-width values in kernel code is a checked method (`checked_*`, or in [`wide`] the `overflowing_*` limb steps, whose carry or borrow is kept), so nothing depends on overflow checks being on: a result that does not fit is `None` or an error, never a silently wrapped value. Only the compiler's evaluation of constants uses native operators, where an overflow stops the build. Counts of steps never saturate: a saturated bound would understate the truth.

No floating-point value produced here from finite inputs is NaN. [`math`] returns a [`real::Real`] or an error; an [`interval::Interval`] has finite bounds or is refused as `NotFinite`; [`eft`] reports a pair that is not exact with an infinite second part.

Every interval operation encloses the exact result of its operation on any reals in its operands, and an enclosure that needs a maths function without a proven error is refused ([`NumError::UnprovenMaths`]).
A bound carries its grid step, and bounds add exactly in the finer step ([`exactness::Exactness`]).

No `unsafe`, no panics outside tests, no platform maths: every maths function comes from [`math`], which uses the pure-Rust `libm` crate; where `libm` uses a processor instruction instead (the square root, and the fused multiply-add where the processor has one), it is one IEEE 754 defines exactly, so results are identical on every target.

modules.cost: constant time and no allocation. Each function is a fixed sequence of floating-point operations, comparisons and bit reads; outside Dekker's direct range `split` also scales by 2^64 and back, and `two_prod` scales by powers of two (`scale`), each scaling at most two steps.
guarantees: **Exact or reported, never silently wrong.** For finite inputs the pair is exact whenever an exact pair exists, and then both parts are finite. When none exists, the second part is an infinity with the sign of the exact error, so one check, `e.is_finite()`, tells a caller whether the pair is exact. No exact pair exists only when the rounded sum or product overflows, when the high half of a split would be ±2^1024, or when the exact error of a product is finer than the smallest subnormal 2^−1074 (possible only for |a · b| < 2^−969). The tests check every case against exact rationals (`num-rational`) on random and adversarial inputs.

**Never NaN from finite inputs.** The second part is NaN only when the first part is NaN: a NaN input, or an IEEE operation on infinities that is itself NaN (∞ − ∞, 0 · ∞). Any other non-finite input gives an infinite second part. So the crate's "never NaN" invariant (`lib.rs`) holds here for every finite input; for infinite inputs it holds except where IEEE 754 itself makes the rounded sum or product NaN.

**The rounded part is the IEEE 754 result.** `s` is `a + b` and `p` is `a * b` as Rust computes them (round to nearest, ties to even). An exact error is at most half a unit in the last place of that result, so the pair does not overlap: `s + e` rounds back to `s`.

**One zero.** A second part that is zero is +0, never −0: the exact error of a sum or a product, and the low half of a split, whatever the signs of the inputs and however Veltkamp's split falls. So the second part depends on the exact pair alone, as an exact zero does in IEEE arithmetic (a zero sum of operands of opposite signs is +0 under round to nearest, IEEE 754-2019, section 6.3) and as it does for a two-product by fused multiply-add. Hence [`fast_two_sum`] and [`two_sum`] agree bit for bit (a NaN aside, whose bits Rust does not fix), and `two_prod(−a, b)` is `(−p, −e)` for a nonzero `e` and `(−p, +0)` for a zero one. Where the last step of an algorithm can give −0, the function adds +0, which turns −0 into +0 and leaves every other value as it is (the proof is on the crate's one helper for it, `zero_to_plus` in `real.rs`, which [`crate::interval`] uses too); each function's documentation shows where that is needed and why it is needed nowhere else.

**Deterministic.** Only `+`, `−`, `×` and `÷` on `f64` (`÷` only by a power of two), comparisons, and reads and writes of a double's bits. Rust computes these to IEEE 754 binary64, each rounded once, on every target the kernel builds for (RFC 3514). The RFC names the exception itself: on 32-bit x86 without SSE2 (the i586 targets) the x87 unit computes with a different precision and so can round twice, which would break these algorithms; the kernel does not support those targets. The RFC also rules out fusing `a * b + c` into one fused multiply-add, which would break them too, and none is used on purpose either: `two_prod` follows Dekker's splitting instead of `mul_add`, which `core` lacks and which is a slow software call on wasm32 (evidence note 05, section 1).

**No integer overflow.** The only integer steps that run are on the 11-bit exponent fields: bit masks, shifts by 52 places that keep the field inside 64 bits, `abs_diff`, which is exact for every input, and `checked_sub`, whose `None` ends a loop. There is no other integer arithmetic at run time (the compiler alone evaluates the checks on the constants, where an overflow would stop the build) and no cast, so nothing here depends on overflow checks being on.

method.text: Dekker 1971 (`fast_two_sum`, Veltkamp's `split`, `two_prod`) and Knuth (`two_sum`), in the form and with the proofs of Shewchuk 1997: Theorem 6 (fast two-sum), Theorem 7 (two-sum), Theorem 17 (split) and Theorem 18 (two-product). Shewchuk's proofs assume an unbounded exponent (his section 2.1 leaves overflow and underflow aside); each function below derives the conditions under which they hold in binary64 and says what it does outside them. `fast_two_sum` puts its operands in the order Dekker's method needs. `two_sum` runs Knuth's six operations and, in the one case where an intermediate overflows, returns `fast_two_sum`'s pair instead. `split` and `two_prod` run Veltkamp's and Dekker's operations unchanged where the conditions hold, and otherwise first move their inputs into that range by exact powers of two, then check that the way back is exact. Shewchuk, "Adaptive precision floating-point arithmetic and fast robust geometric predicates", *Discrete & Computational Geometry* 18 (1997), 305–363, <https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009321>. D. E. Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, volume 2, section 4.2.2. S. Boldo, "Pitfalls of a full floating-point proof: example on the formal proof of the Veltkamp/Dekker algorithms", *Automated Reasoning* (IJCAR 2006), Lecture Notes in Computer Science 4130: Veltkamp's high half is the input rounded to nearest. modules.cost: constant time and no allocation per operation; [`Interval::norm`] is linear in its number of components.
guarantees: **Inclusion**, as above, for `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `div`, `mul_add`, `square`, `sqrt`, `norm` and `neg`. These are built from the operations IEEE 754 rounds correctly, so one step outward is a proven enclosure. An enclosure that needs a function whose error `libm` does not prove (`sin`, `cos`, `atan2`, `exp`, `ln`) is refused with [`NumError::UnprovenMaths`] until proven versions exist (build piece G47).

**Finite, ordered, never NaN.** Both bounds are finite and `lo ≤ hi`. An operation whose widened bound would leave the finite doubles (a rounded bound that reaches ±(2 − 2^−52) · 2^1023 or overflows) returns [`NumError::NotFinite`] instead.

**Tight.** Each computed bound is the first or second double beyond the exact bound of the operation over its operands, never farther: the rounding lands on the exact bound or on one of the two doubles either side of it, and the widening moves one double outward. So the lower bound is at least the double below the largest double at or below the exact lower bound, and the upper bound at most the double above the smallest double at or above the exact upper bound. A bound that is exact by construction is not widened, so it is the exact bound itself: both bounds of `neg`, the lower bound 0 of `square` over an interval holding zero, and a zero bound of `sqrt`. `norm` chains several operations, so each of its steps is tight in this sense but the whole is not. Counted in steps, where the step at a value is the spacing of the doubles in its binade, a computed bound is at most 2.5 steps of the exact bound outside it, at most 2 steps of the computed bound, less than 2 steps of the larger of the two, and at most 1.5 steps when the two steps are equal. The first two maxima are reached at ties next to a power of two, where the spacing halves: 1 + (−2^−54) = 1 − 2^−54 is a tie that rounds to the even 1 and is widened to 1 + 2^−52, which is 2.5 steps of 2^−53 (the spacing just below 1) above the exact value; and 1 + 2^−53 is a tie that also rounds to 1 and is widened to 1 − 2^−53, exactly 2 steps of 2^−53 (the spacing at that bound) below the exact value.

**Deterministic.** Only IEEE 754 basic operations and comparisons, which Rust computes to IEEE 754 binary64 on every target the kernel builds for (RFC 3514, whose own exception, 32-bit x86 without SSE2, is not one of them); `next_up` and `next_down`, which are integer operations on the bits; and the square root and fused multiply-add of [`crate::math`]. The fused multiply-add is `libm` 0.2.16's `fma`, correctly rounded as IEEE 754 requires whether `libm` uses the processor's instruction or its own routine. That root is not Rust's but `libm` 0.2.16's `sqrt`, which is the processor's IEEE 754 square root on x86-64 (`sqrtsd`, with SSE2) and on aarch64 (`fsqrt`, with NEON), and on wasm32 libm's portable integer routine (`src/math/generic/sqrt.rs`: Goldschmidt iterations, then musl's decision of the last bit), because libm uses WebAssembly's square root instruction only with its `unstable-intrinsics` feature, which is off. IEEE 754 requires the square root to be correctly rounded, and the portable routine is written to the same result, so every route gives the same bits. Inclusion for the roots needs only a faithful root; equality across targets needs the correctly rounded one, which on wasm32 rests on libm's routine rather than on hardware, and libm's own comments rest that routine's last bit on testing, not on a proof. So `tests/attack2_interval.rs` holds `math::sqrt` bit for bit to an exact oracle (roots within a tiny fraction of a unit of a midpoint, subnormal operands, exact roots), and CI runs it on wasm32-wasip1 too (`.github/workflows/kernel.yml`). Minimum and maximum are written as comparisons, not with `f64::min` and `f64::max`, which may return either zero when given −0 and +0. A zero bound is always stored as +0, so equal intervals have equal bits whatever their history.
modules.job: Intervals of doubles that certainly contain an exact real result, in round-to-nearest arithmetic.

method.text: interval arithmetic in round-to-nearest with outward widening, as in Geogram's `intervalRN` (after Harris) and in CGAL's widening with `nextafter` when it cannot change the rounding mode. Harris widens each bound by the relative factor 1 ± 2^−52, a second rounded operation; this module moves each bound by exactly one step, which is tighter and needs no further rounding. The square is the interval power of Moore, Kearfott and Cloud, which is IEEE Std 1788-2015's `sqr`: over an interval holding zero x² is smallest at zero, otherwise at the bound nearer zero, and largest at the bound farther from zero. The roots follow IEEE Std 1788-2015's `sqrt`, whose domain is [0, +∞): `sqrt` refuses an operand that reaches outside the domain, and the private root inside `norm` is the standard's set-based evaluation over the part of the operand inside it. The length is the natural interval extension of √(c₁² + … + cₙ²) (Moore, Kearfott and Cloud), built from those operations. The fused multiply-add is the natural extension of x · y + z over the box of operands, with IEEE 754's correctly rounded `fusedMultiplyAdd` (IEEE 754-2019, section 5.4.1) at the corners. R. Harris, "Why interval arithmetic won't cure your floating point blues", *Overload* 19(103), June 2011, <https://accu.org/journals/overload/19/103/harris_1974/>. Geogram `interval_nt.h` (BSD-3-Clause), the round-to-nearest `intervalRN` class: <https://github.com/BrunoLevy/geogram/blob/40d72165ceeeb0a61977d6fdf74d929bfdd77b7b/src/lib/geogram/numerics/interval_nt.h#L455-L462>. CGAL `FPU.h`, widening with `nextafter`: <https://github.com/CGAL/cgal/blob/cbc3b81d4607c6f3a9d1f3a47d8709a2be3e6bfa/Number_types/include/CGAL/FPU.h#L347-L358>. R. E. Moore, R. B. Kearfott and M. J. Cloud, *Introduction to Interval Analysis*, SIAM, 2009: the integer power of an interval and the natural interval extension of an expression. IEEE Std 1788-2015, *IEEE Standard for Interval Arithmetic*: the required elementary functions `sqr` and `sqrt`, the set-based flavour, and the decoration `trv` that reports a cut domain. `libm` 0.2.16 (MIT), `src/math/sqrt.rs`, `src/math/arch/` and `src/math/generic/sqrt.rs`: <https://github.com/rust-lang/compiler-builtins/tree/dfd2203a4d6110820ad7bb65cafe1bf331a03a3d/libm/src/math>.

modules.cost: constant time and no allocation. Every function is a fixed number of products and sums in `i128` and fixed-width integers: [`Plane::side_of_tpi`] is four products in [`I384`] after the point's homogeneous coordinates, repeated in [`I512`] only on the total path; [`Tpi::to_grid`] is one restoring long division per coordinate, 40 steps when the point lies within the frame's range and at most 127 otherwise, each step a few operations on six or eight 64-bit limbs.
guarantees: Every result is exact, or an error. A [`Sign`] is decided by integer arithmetic alone; no rounding ever decides it. Only [`Tpi::to_grid`] rounds: it rounds the exact rational point to the nearest grid point (ties to even) and says whether it rounded, moving each coordinate by at most [`COMMIT_PER_AXIS`](crate::ladder::COMMIT_PER_AXIS), half a step.

Nothing overflows, and nothing could wrap silently if it did. A [`Plane`] can only be made by [`Plane::through`] from grid points (within 2^40 − 1 steps of the origin), which checks the plane's budget below at construction (chapter 6.2); a [`Tpi`] can only be made by [`Tpi::new`], which checks that its homogeneous coordinates fit their types. Every intermediate fits its type by the derivation written on each function; the arithmetic of every derivation, and every figure in the table below, is asserted when the crate compiles (the budget exponents in the source, from `GRID_DIFFERENCE_BITS` on); and every operation, on `i128` and on wide integers alike, is checked, so none of this depends on a build with overflow checks. In summary, with B = 40 and every coordinate below 2^B in magnitude: | Quantity | Bound | Type | | --- | --- | --- | | Plane normal n | 2^(2B+3) = 2^83 | `i128` | | Plane offset d | 2^(3B+5) = 2^125 | `i128` | | Grid point against a plane, n · p + d | 2^126 | `i128` | | Three-plane denominator w | 2^(6B+12) = 2^252 | [`I256`] | | Three-plane numerators X | 2^(7B+14) = 2^294 | [`I320`] | | Three-plane point against a plane, n · X + d · w | 2^(9B+19) = 2^379 | [`I384`] | At B = 26 the same formulas give 9B + 19 = 253 bits, within the 256 bits EMBER uses for its 26-bit inputs (evidence note 05, section 4). The bounds are safe rather than tight: they bound every factor separately, and a triangle inside the frame cannot make every product maximal at once. With M = 2^40 − 1, what grid points can reach is |`n_i`| ≤ 4M² and |d| ≤ 4M³ (82 and 122 bits; derivations on [`Plane::through`]), |n · p + d| ≤ 16M³ (124 bits, on [`Plane::side`]), and from the plane bounds, because each of w, `X_i` and n · X + d · w is a determinant whose largest magnitude over a box of entries lies at a corner of the box, |w| ≤ 256M^6, |`X_i`| ≤ 256M^7 and |n · X + d · w| ≤ 4096M^9 (248, 288 and 372 bits; derivations on [`Tpi::homogeneous`] and [`Plane::side_of_tpi`]). Planes and three-plane points built from the corners of the frame's cube reach every one of these exactly (tested).
Deterministic: integers only, no floating point, no platform maths, no allocation.

method.text: plane-based geometry with vertices as three-plane intersections in homogeneous integer coordinates, as in Campen and Kobbelt 2010 ([doi:10.1111/j.1467-8659.2009.01609.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2009.01609.x)), Nehring-Wirxel, Trettner and Kobbelt 2021 ([doi:10.1016/j.cad.2021.103015](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cad.2021.103015)) and EMBER 2022 (Trettner, Nehring-Wirxel and Kobbelt, [doi:10.1145/3528223.3530181](https://doi.org/10.1145/3528223.3530181)). Classifying a homogeneous point by multiplying by the sign of w, so that nothing is divided, follows Attene 2020's indirect predicates ([doi:10.1016/j.cad.2020.102856](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cad.2020.102856); method only, re-derived here). The rounding division is restoring binary long division (Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, volume 2, section 4.3.1). The reach of the bounds uses Hadamard's determinant inequality (J. Hadamard, 1893, *Bulletin des Sciences Mathématiques* 17).

guarantees: **Exact for every input.** No rounding ever decides a sign, and `Zero` means exactly degenerate. Each predicate documents its degenerate cases, including which sign a degenerate but non-zero answer has.

**The same answer in every build profile; no overflow, no panic.** Outside its tests this module uses no native `+`, `-` or `*` on a fixed-width integer, and no cast: every operation is a checked method (`checked_sub`, `checked_mul`, `checked_add`, `checked_neg`) that returns `None` instead of wrapping. So nothing here depends on overflow checks being on, which they are not in a default release build. `tests/attack_predicate.rs` scans this file's code to keep it that way.
**Deterministic.** Integer arithmetic only: the same answer on every target.
modules.job: Exact geometric predicates on grid points: orientation in 2D and 3D, in-circle and in-sphere.

method.text: the determinant forms of Shewchuk, *Adaptive Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic and Fast Robust Geometric Predicates*, Discrete & Computational Geometry 18 (1997) (<https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009321>; reference code <https://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/project/quake/public/code/predicates.c>): orientation is the determinant of the edge vectors, and in-circle and in-sphere are the orientation of the points lifted onto the paraboloid z = |p|², written relative to the query point so every entry is a small difference. Shewchuk evaluates these in floating point with adaptive expansions; on the grid the inputs are integers below 2^40, so the same determinants evaluate exactly in fixed-width integers. There is no floating-point filter yet: a generated filter (chapter 6.2) is a later piece, and it may only ever return early with the sign this exact path gives. The total path's bounds follow the static bit-length analysis of Fortune and Van Wyk, *Static Analysis Yields Efficient Exact Integer Arithmetic for Computational Geometry*, ACM Transactions on Graphics 15(3) (1996), carried in Rust's type system so that the compiler checks them.

**The same data on every target.** Test data comes from integer arithmetic only, and every word drawn from proptest's stream is a whole `u64`, so a seed gives the same inputs on every target, 32-bit and 64-bit, and only the kernel's results can differ. Golden hashes in [`grid`] and [`prop`] check it, and CI runs them natively and under wasm32-wasip1.

Each coordinate is one of: full range (2 in 8 draws); small, in −16..=16; one of the extremes ±(2^40 − 1), ±(2^40 − 2), 0 and ±1; snapped to a coarse sub-grid (1 mm, 2.5 mm, 0.01 mm at the building step, 1 mm at the mechanical step, 2^20 steps, 625 steps) so coincident faces and shared edges are common; snapped and then moved by exactly one step, so near-coincidences are common; a repeat of an earlier coordinate; or an earlier coordinate moved by one step. Each point is fresh (half the draws), a repeat of an earlier point, an earlier point moved one step along one axis, a point on the line through the two latest points (so the next point of a triangle is often collinear with the first two), or a point on the line through two earlier points. modules.cost: linear in the expression's length to parse; O(n log n) in its operands to canonicalise.
modules.does: [`Expr::parse`] reads an SPDX licence expression as Cargo manifests carry it. [`Expr::permissive`] says whether it can be met with permissive licences alone, and [`Expr::canonical`] writes it in one form per meaning, so two records can be compared. [`records`] reads the licence records of a crate header: the list items after its `Licences` line, each of the form ``- <expression>: `package`, `package` and `package`.``
guarantees: **Exact grammar, or an error.** An expression with an unknown character, an unbalanced parenthesis, a missing operand or a stray operator is an [`ExprError`], never a pass.

**Permissive means every licence of one way to comply is permissive.** An `OR` needs one permissive branch, an `AND` needs both, and `WITH` may add only an exception in [`EXCEPTIONS`], which grant permissions and take none away. So `MIT OR Apache-2.0 OR LGPL-2.1-or-later` is permissive, taken under MIT or Apache-2.0, and `MIT AND GPL-3.0-only` is not. The permissive licences are exactly [`PERMISSIVE`]: the list the development crates may take (MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD, ISC, Zlib, Unicode). The Unlicense is not on it (chapter 32.6 takes it only beside another licence), nor is MPL-2.0, which is ours and is checked separately.

**One form per meaning.** [`Expr::canonical`] flattens nested `OR`s and `AND`s and sorts and deduplicates their operands, so `MIT OR Apache-2.0`, `Apache-2.0 OR MIT` and Cargo's legacy `MIT/Apache-2.0` compare equal.
modules.job: Licences: whether a package's licence expression is permissive, and the licence records every development crate keeps in its header.

method.text: the SPDX license expression grammar of the SPDX specification 2.3, annex D (<https://spdx.github.io/spdx-spec/v2.3/SPDX-license-expressions/>), by recursive descent, with its precedence (`WITH` binds tightest, then `AND`, then `OR`) and Cargo's legacy `/` read as `OR` (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-license-and-license-file-fields>). Recursion is bounded: nesting deeper than [`MAX_DEPTH`] parentheses is an error.

[`repo`] reads the input from a workspace on disk (the crates under `projects/engines/geometry/crates`, and the facade `engine-geometry` and its binding crates under `projects/engines/crates`) and writes or checks the committed map; the binary `map` (`cargo run -p geom-test --bin map -- check`) runs it in CI. The map lists each crate's job, layer, invariants, sections, family, status and published dependencies; each module's job, what it does, guarantees, method with its links, cost and family; every provenance record, merged into one entry per source; and every error kind of each kernel crate.
guarantees: **One map per source tree.** The text depends only on the files read: crates in name order, modules in path order, fields in a fixed order, object keys sorted, list items in header order, no timestamps, no absolute paths (every path is relative to the workspace root, with `/`), and `\n` line ends. The same tree gives the same bytes on every target.
**Every problem names its file and field.** A [`Problem`] carries the file's path, the [`Rule`] (the field of the grammar) and what to write; nothing stops at the first problem.

**Known gaps are visible, exact and cannot rot.** A problem listed in [`GAPS`] (or the gaps a test passes) by its file, rule and exact message is not reported, but the map lists the gap with its reason; any other problem in the same file and rule is still reported, and a gap that no longer occurs is itself a problem ([`Rule::GapStale`]), as the scaffold check's header gaps work.

**One record per source.** Records are merged by how the source was taken and the source's link without its fragment, so one file at one commit is one source whatever line range a header shows; two headers that give one source different licences are a problem in each, not a silent choice (29.20, rule 1).

[`view`] reads a web address on a code-hosting site into the repository it names, the revision it names and whether it shows code. [`is_code`] says whether an address points at source code, [`is_pinned`] whether it names a full commit, [`repository`] which repository or file it belongs to (so a credit line can be matched with a link elsewhere), and [`source_key`] which source it is (one file at one revision, whatever line range it shows).
guarantees: **Every link once, in order.** A link that appears twice is listed once, at its first place.
**Trailing punctuation is not part of a link.** A sentence's `.`, `,`, `;` or `:` after an address, and the `>` or `)` that closes it, are left out.

**A DOI is a whole DOI.** `doi:10.` must be followed by a registrant code (digits, with sub-divisions after full stops), a `/` and a suffix that is not empty; a `doi.org` address is a link only when its path is such a DOI.

**Every code host's layout, read by its revision slot.** A link is on a code-hosting site when its host is one of [`FORGE_HOSTS`], starts with one of [`FORGE_HOST_PREFIXES`] or ends with one of [`FORGE_HOST_SUFFIXES`], or when its path or query has one of the layouts below, on any host. It is pinned when the revision slot of its layout, and only that slot, is a full commit name: 40 hexadecimal digits for SHA-1 or 64 for SHA-256, in lower case. - GitHub's layout, shared by Gitea, Forgejo, Codeberg, Gitee, Bitbucket, sourcehut and `SourceForge`: `<owner>/<repository>/<view>/<revision>/<path>`, a view one of [`VIEWS`] (Gitea's `src/commit/<revision>`, `src/branch/…` and `src/tag/…` included); `raw.githubusercontent.com/<owner>/<repository>/<revision>/<path>`; and gists, `gist.github.com/<user>/<id>/<revision>`. - GitLab's, on any host: `<group>/…/<repository>/-/<view>/<revision>/<path>`. - Gitiles' (`*.googlesource.com` and any Gerrit host): `<repository>/+/<revision>/<path>`, and its other `+` commands. - cgit's (hosts starting `cgit.` or `git.`, or a `cgit` path segment): `<repository>/<view>/<path>?id=<revision>`; without an `id`, GitHub's revision slot. - gitweb's, on any host: `?p=<repository>;a=<action>;f=<path>;hb=<revision>`.

**Conservative about code.** An address is code when it shows a file, folder, commit or diff in a repository on a code-hosting site, when it is a gist, or when its last path segment, or a value in its query, ends in one of [`CODE_EXTENSIONS`] (`.rs.html` and other source pages included). modules.cost: one run of the property per case, plus shrinking after a failure, at most about 41 property runs per coordinate (a binary search over at most 2^40 magnitudes). One read of proptest's process-wide configuration per [`run`] or [`first_value`].
modules.does: [`run`] runs a proptest property from a [`Seed`] resolved and printed by [`crate::seed::resolve`], so a property test has the same seed rules as every other seeded test. [`config`] builds the proptest configuration it uses. [`first_value`] draws one case from a seed. [`coord`], [`p2`] and [`p3`] are proptest strategies for grid coordinates and points.
guarantees: **The seed decides every case, or nothing runs.** [`config`] fixes the seed, the generator (`ChaCha20`) and every runner setting that changes which cases are drawn or how they shrink, so proptest's runner variables (`PROPTEST_RNG_SEED`, `PROPTEST_RNG_ALGORITHM`, `PROPTEST_CASES`, `PROPTEST_MAX_SHRINK_ITERS` and the other limits) cannot change a run: `SPAREKIT_SEED` is the one override. That is why [`run`] drives proptest's `TestRunner` directly; the `proptest!` macro re-reads those variables after its configuration is built. Two settings cannot be fixed that way, so [`run`] and [`first_value`] refuse to draw anything, with [`Failure::Environment`], while either is in force: - `PROPTEST_MAX_DEFAULT_SIZE_RANGE`. proptest 1.12 reads it once per process into `Config::default()`, and every collection strategy of default size (`any::<Vec<T>>()`, `any::<String>()`, `vec(s, SizeRange::default())`) takes its size from there when the strategy is built, before [`run`] sees it (`collection.rs`, `impl Default for SizeRange`). A runner's own `max_default_size_range` is never read. So a seed printed in a shell with the variable set would draw other cases in a shell without it. Strategies with explicit sizes (`vec(s, 0..=n)`) never read it. - Forking and timeouts (`PROPTEST_FORK`, `PROPTEST_TIMEOUT`, read when another crate in the build turns on proptest's `fork` or `timeout` feature). A forked case runs in another process, and a timeout lets a clock decide a result (28.19).

**The same cases on every target.** These strategies draw exactly one 64-bit word from proptest's `ChaCha20` stream per coordinate and make the coordinate from it with [`crate::rng::SplitMix64`], in integer arithmetic only. proptest's own samplers are not used for them: proptest 1.12 samples a `usize` range as a `u64` on 64-bit targets and as a `u32` on 32-bit ones (`num.rs`, `sample_uniform!`), so `proptest::sample::select`, for one, reads the stream at different offsets on wasm32 and on x86-64, and every later value of the case differs. A strategy a caller builds from proptest's samplers keeps that weakness; a test whose cases must replay across targets draws from these strategies or from [`crate::grid`].

**No files.** Failure persistence is off: a run never reads or writes `proptest-regressions` files, so its result depends only on the seed and the code. A failure becomes a permanent fixture by the route of 28.16, not by a file proptest keeps.
**A failure carries its replay.** [`Failure`] names the property, the seed, the minimal failing input after shrinking, and the `SPAREKIT_SEED` value that replays it.

**Grid strategies stay on the grid and shrink towards zero.** Every value has magnitude at most [`COORD_MAX`]. A coordinate shrinks by binary search from its drawn value towards zero, whichever kind of value was drawn, so for a property that fails exactly when |v| ≥ k (k > 0) the minimal failing coordinate proptest reports is ±k.
modules.job: Property tests run from a seed: proptest with the seed discipline, and grid strategies that draw the same cases on every target.

method.text: proptest (MIT OR Apache-2.0, <https://github.com/proptest-rs/proptest>), the Hypothesis-style property tester the kernel's tests use (28.2). Its runner draws each case from a `ChaCha20` stream seeded by `RngSeed::Fixed`, and shrinks a failure to a minimal case. A coordinate shrinks with proptest's own `num::i64::BinarySearch`, which halves the distance towards zero while the property still fails and backs off when it passes: bisection, as in Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, volume 3, section 6.2.1 (<https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html>).

modules.cost: a handful of integer operations per word. [`SplitMix64::below`] draws one word, and draws again with probability below `n / 2^64`, so fewer than two words on average.
modules.does: [`SplitMix64`] turns a [`Seed`] into a stream of 64-bit words. [`ByteSource`] turns a fuzzer's bytes into the same kind of stream. Both implement [`Entropy`], so one builder (for example [`crate::grid::GridSampler`]) makes test data from a seed in a property test and from coverage-guided bytes in a fuzz target.
guarantees: **The same words on every target.** `SplitMix64` is wrapping 64-bit integer arithmetic only, so a seed gives the same stream on every target, in every build profile.

**Every word, once per period.** The state is a counter advanced by an odd constant, so it visits all 2^64 values once per period, and the output function is a bijection of the state, so over one period every 64-bit word is returned exactly once.
**Unbiased bounded draws.** [`SplitMix64::below`] returns each value in `0..n` with exactly equal probability over the generator's period.

**Test only, and independent of the kernel.** The kernel has no randomness (28.17); this is not the counter-based generator chapter 27 plans for `geom-num`, so a change there never changes a test's inputs. It is not cryptographic and must never seed anything that ships.
**[`ByteSource`] never fails.** Past the end of its bytes it yields zeros, so every input, including the empty one, decodes to some test case.
modules.job: `SplitMix64`, the deterministic generator behind every seeded test input, and [`Entropy`], the source of words that test-data builders draw from.

method.text: `SplitMix64` of Steele, Lea and Flood, "Fast Splittable Pseudorandom Number Generators", OOPSLA 2014 (<https://doi.org/10.1145/2660193.2660195>), with the constants of Vigna's reference implementation `splitmix.c` (<https://prng.di.unimi.it/splitmix.c>, public domain): the golden-ratio increment `0x9e3779b97f4a7c15` and Stafford's "Mix13" output function (<https://zimbry.blogspot.com/2011/09/better-bit-mixing-improving-on.html>). The unit tests check it against 50 outputs of that reference implementation. Bounded draws use Lemire's multiply-and-reject method, "Fast Random Integer Generation in an Interval", ACM Transactions on Modeling and Computer Simulation 29(1), 2019 (<https://doi.org/10.1145/3230636>).

modules.cost: constant time; one environment read per [`resolve`], none for [`fixed`].
modules.does: a [`Seed`] is a 64-bit value that decides every input a seeded test draws. [`resolve`] picks a test's seed, the value of the environment variable [`ENV_VAR`] (`SPAREKIT_SEED`) when it is set and the test's fixed default otherwise, and prints it as `seed: <hex>` before the test draws anything. [`fixed`] prints a seed that a test must use whatever the environment says, because its assertions depend on that seed (a golden hash, a recorded case).
guarantees: **Every seed is printed.** [`resolve`] and [`fixed`] print one line that starts `seed: ` and is followed by exactly 16 lowercase hexadecimal digits, then the test's label, where the seed came from and how to replay it. Rust's test harness shows a passing test's output only with `--nocapture`, and always shows a failing test's, so every failure carries its seed (28.5: "Every generator prints its seed, so any failure replays exactly").

**Any printed seed replays exactly.** Setting `SPAREKIT_SEED` to the digits [`resolve`] printed makes it return the same seed, and the generators in [`crate::rng`] then give the same inputs on every target. A seed [`fixed`] printed replays by itself: the test always uses it.

**A seed is never invented here.** It is the test's fixed default or the value of `SPAREKIT_SEED`; nothing reads a clock or the operating system's random source. Pull requests run with the fixed defaults; a nightly job sets `SPAREKIT_SEED` to a fresh value, and the printed line logs it (28.17).
**A malformed override is an error, never ignored.** A run that asked for one seed and silently got another would replay the wrong case, so [`resolve`] returns [`SeedError`] instead.
